statement: Which of these shapes has exactly one line of symmetry?

choices.misconception: I noticed only the line straight down the middle, but a square folds onto itself in 4 different ways.

choices.text: a rectangle that is not a square
choices.misconception: I checked only the fold from top to bottom, but a rectangle also folds onto itself from side to side, so it has 2 lines.

choices.text: a triangle with all three sides equal
choices.misconception: I checked only the line from the top corner down, but each corner has a line like that, which makes 3.

choices.text: a parallelogram with no right angles and with two long and two short sides
choices.misconception: I thought folding along a diagonal matches the two halves, but they only match after a half turn, so it has no line of symmetry.

choices.text: a triangle with exactly two equal sides

hints: Imagine folding each shape so the two halves match exactly.
A line of symmetry is a fold that puts one half exactly on top of the other. For each shape, count every such fold, not just the first one you notice.

Square: 4 folds. Rectangle: 2. Triangle with three equal sides: 3. Slanted parallelogram: 0, since a diagonal fold does not match. Triangle with exactly two equal sides: just 1, through the corner between the equal sides.

solutions.reliable: Count the folds that match exactly. A square has 4 (two through the middles of opposite sides, two along the diagonals). A rectangle that is not a square has 2. A triangle with three equal sides has 3. A slanted parallelogram has none: folding along a diagonal does not make the halves line up. A triangle with exactly two equal sides has exactly 1, from the corner between the equal sides to the middle of the opposite side. The transferable idea: a line of symmetry is a fold that matches exactly, so test every possible fold before deciding.

whyOnTest: It checks that symmetry means a fold that matches exactly, and that students count every fold rather than stopping at the first, or seeing one in a parallelogram.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
